report:
Contrary to the view that olive leaf extract (OLE) has no effect, scientific evidence indicates that OLE **can lower blood pressure**, particularly in individuals with pre-hypertension or stage-1 hypertension.

### Key Evidence
1. **Clinical Trial Results:** A double-blind randomized clinical trial compared OLE (500 mg twice daily) to Captopril (a standard ACE inhibitor) in stage-1 hypertensive patients. Both groups experienced significant and comparable reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure over eight weeks (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21036583/).
2. **Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses:** Syntheses of randomized controlled trials report that OLE supplementation (typically 1,000 mg daily, rich in the active compound oleuropein) produces statistically significant blood pressure reductions—lowering systolic pressure by up to ~11.5 mmHg and diastolic pressure by ~4.6 mmHg (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ptr.8509, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13098-022-00920-y).
3. **Mechanisms:** OLE polyphenols act as antioxidants and encourage endothelial vasodilation, contributing to reduced vascular resistance (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8137474/).

### Limitations
While studies demonstrate antihypertensive effects, individual clinical trials are modest in size and length. Major clinical guidelines do not recommend OLE as a direct substitute for standard prescription therapies, though it shows potential as a complementary intervention under medical supervision.
